title: Chapter 59 — Squid
paragraphs: Slowly wading through the meadows of brit, the Pequod still held her course northeast toward the island of Java. A gentle breeze pushed her keel, so that in the surrounding calm her three tall tapering masts swayed mildly to the lazy wind, like three palm trees on a plain. And still, at wide intervals in the silvery night, the lonely, beckoning jet would be seen.

But one transparent blue morning, when a stillness almost supernatural spread over the sea — a calm, yet not a stagnant one — when the long burnished sun-glare on the waters seemed a golden finger laid across them, commanding some secrecy, when the slippered waves whispered together as they softly ran on — in this profound hush of the visible world, a strange apparition was seen by Daggoo from the main-masthead.

In the distance, a great white mass lazily rose, and rising higher and higher, disentangling itself from the blue, at last gleamed before our bow like a snow-slide, freshly slipped from the hills. Thus glistening for a moment, it slowly sank. Then once more it arose and silently gleamed. It did not seem a whale — and yet, was this Moby Dick? thought Daggoo. Again the phantom went down, but reappearing once more, with a stiletto-like cry that startled every man from his drowse, the harpooner shouted, "There! There again! There she breaches! Right ahead! The White Whale, the White Whale!"

Upon this, the seamen rushed to the yardarms, as in swarming-time the bees rush to the branches. Bareheaded in the sultry sun, Ahab stood on the bowsprit, and with one hand pushed far behind him in readiness to wave orders to the helmsman, he cast his eager glance in the direction indicated aloft by the outstretched, motionless arm of Daggoo.

Whether the constant attendance of that one still and solitary jet had gradually worked upon Ahab, so that he was now prepared to connect the ideas of gentleness and calm with the first sight of the particular whale he hunted — however this was, or whether his eagerness misled him — whichever way it might have been, no sooner did he clearly perceive the white mass than with fierce intensity he instantly gave orders for lowering.

The four boats were soon on the water, Ahab's in advance, all swiftly pulling toward their prey. Soon it went down. And while, with oars suspended, we were awaiting its reappearance — there, in the same spot where it sank, once more it slowly rose. Almost forgetting for the moment all thoughts of Moby Dick, we now gazed at the most wondrous phenomenon which the secret seas have ever revealed to humankind. A vast pulpy mass, furlongs in length and breadth, of a gleaming cream-color, lay floating on the water, with innumerable long arms radiating from its center, curling and twisting like a nest of anacondas, as if blindly to clutch at any unlucky object within reach. No perceptible face or front had it. No imaginable mouth. But it looked like a formless, chance-like thing of unearthly life.

As with a low sucking sound it slowly disappeared again, Starbuck, still gazing at the agitated waters where it had sunk, exclaimed with a wild voice — "I almost would rather have seen Moby Dick and fought him, than to have seen you, white ghost!"
"The great live squid, which, they say, few whale-ships have ever seen and returned to their ports to tell of it."
But Ahab said nothing. Turning his boat, he sailed back to the vessel. The rest silently followed.

Whatever superstitions the sperm whalemen in general have connected with the sight of this creature, it is certain that a glimpse of it being so very unusual, that fact has gone far to invest it with ominous significance. So rarely is it seen that, though every whaleman declares it to be the largest living thing in the ocean, very few of them have any but the vaguest ideas about its true nature and form. Nevertheless, they believe it furnishes the sperm whale with his only food. For though other kinds of whales feed on a diet of small organisms, the sperm whale is known to prey on nothing smaller than the squid.

There seems some ground for imagining that the great Kraken of Bishop Pontoppidan may ultimately turn out to be a squid. The way the Bishop describes it — as alternately rising and sinking, with certain other details he provides — in all this, the two correspond. But much allowance must be made for the incredible size he assigns it.

By some naturalists who have vaguely heard rumors of the mysterious creature spoken of here, it is classified among the cuttlefish, to which, indeed, in certain outward ways it would seem to belong — but only as the giant among its tribe.
